concepts.title: Scalars, Vectors and Their Addition
concepts.definition: A scalar carries only magnitude, while a vector carries magnitude and direction and obeys triangle (or parallelogram) law addition: place vectors head to tail and the closing side from start to finish is the resultant. Two vectors add to zero only when they are equal in size and opposite in direction.
concepts.key_idea: Vectors add geometrically, not arithmetically -- direction is part of the quantity.

solution_steps.explain: Draw the first vector, then start the second where the first ends; the order does not matter.
The vector from the free tail to the free head is the resultant sum.
If the two vectors are opposite and equal, the triangle closes on itself and the resultant is the null vector.

concepts.title: Resolution into Components and Vector Magnitude
concepts.definition: Any plane vector can be split into two perpendicular pieces: an x-component and a y-component whose vector sum rebuilds the original. Conversely the magnitude of a vector comes from its components through the Pythagorean relation, the square root of x squared plus y squared.
concepts.key_idea: Split along the axes, do arithmetic on each axis separately, then reassemble by Pythagoras.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph103.txt lines 161-240 (section 3.5 resolution of vectors, unit vectors i j k, components along axes)

solution_steps.explain: Each component is squared in preparation for the Pythagorean sum.
The root of the summed squares is the vector's magnitude.

concepts.title: Motion in a Plane with Constant Acceleration
concepts.definition: Plane motion with constant acceleration behaves like two independent straight-line motions running side by side -- one per axis. Each coordinate follows the one-dimensional constant-acceleration equations with its own component of initial velocity and the shared acceleration vector.
concepts.key_idea: Horizontal and vertical are separate films played at once -- constant acceleration never mixes the axes.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph103.txt lines 241-320 (section 3.8 motion in a plane with constant acceleration, analogy with 1D motion, component equations)

solution_steps.explain: Write position, velocity and acceleration through their x and y components.
Each axis independently obeys the constant-acceleration relations, using that axis's components.
The plane motion is the vector sum of the two axis solutions; the path can curve even while acceleration is constant.

concepts.title: Projectile Motion: Range and Time of Flight
concepts.definition: A projectile launched over level ground carries a steady horizontal component and a vertical component fighting gravity. The flight time comes from the vertical component alone, and multiplying it by the horizontal component gives the horizontal range; the highest point is reached when the vertical component dies to zero.
concepts.key_idea: Vertical motion sets the clock; horizontal motion sets the distance -- gravity reads only the vertical film.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph103.txt lines 321-420 (section 3.9 projectile motion, equation of path, time of flight, maximum height, horizontal range)
question_patterns: find the time of flight of a projectile launched with the given components

solution_steps.explain: The vertical component spends itself against gravity twice -- rising then falling -- so flight time is twice the vertical component over gravity.
The horizontal component rides for the whole flight time, covering the range.

concepts.title: Uniform Circular Motion and Centripetal Acceleration
concepts.definition: A body sweeping a circle at constant speed still accelerates, because its direction keeps turning: the acceleration points to the centre and has size speed squared over radius. Angular velocity, the rate of turning measured in radians per second, ties the linear speed to the circle size through speed = radius times angular velocity.
concepts.key_idea: Constant speed on a circle is accelerated motion -- the pull toward the centre bends the velocity without changing its size.

solution_steps.explain: The acceleration grows with the square of the tangential speed.
Dividing by the circle's radius gives the centre-directed acceleration.
